section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Wave Nature of Light
section_1.content: Briefly introduce the wave property of light (superposition and interference). Establish that light travels as a wave with phase and amplitude, which is the foundational requirement for understanding holography.
section_1.example: Visualizing ripples in a pond colliding: when two peaks meet, they form a larger peak (constructive interference).

section_2.title: Understanding Diffraction: The 'Bending' Phenomenon
section_2.content: Explain how light waves encounter obstacles or apertures and bend around them. Use Huygens-Fresnel principle to explain how every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
section_2.example: A laser pointer shining through a tiny pinhole creates a spread-out pattern of light rings (Airy disk) rather than just a dot.

section_3.title: The Holographic Recording Process
section_3.content: Describe the split-beam method. The reference beam and object beam intersect at the recording medium. The resulting interference pattern (diffraction grating) encodes both amplitude and phase information.
section_3.example: Imagine a 'Spider-Man' hologram: one laser beam hits Spidey (object beam) and another hits the film directly (reference beam), creating a complex 'fingerprint' of light.

section_4.title: Reconstruction: Decoding the Diffraction Pattern
section_4.content: Explain that when the reference beam shines back through the interference pattern, diffraction occurs. The light is bent exactly as it was when it reflected off the original object, recreating the 3D wavefront.
section_4.example: Shining a flashlight through a piece of glass etched with the interference pattern to make the 3D ghost of a mechanical owl appear to hover in mid-air.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Conclude by emphasizing that holography is essentially 'frozen diffraction.' Connect this to modern uses: security features on credit cards, high-density data storage, and medical imaging.
section_5.example: Visualizing a credit card security hologram where the 'Dove' logo changes perspective as you tilt the card, proving the 3D spatial storage of the image.
